title: The Plagues of Egypt
lead: The ten blows on Egypt before the exodus (Exodus 7–12), recalled in Psalms 78 and 105 and reused in Revelation's trumpets and bowls.

sections.b: Israel's poets retell the plagues in their own order and number. Psalm 78:43–51 lists seven or eight, beginning with blood and ending with the firstborn; Psalm 105:26–36 lists eight, starting with darkness. The Philistines tremble at the memory of the God who struck Egypt (1 Samuel 4:8; 6:6). Deuteronomy turns the plagues into a warning for Israel itself: "the diseases of Egypt" will come on a faithless people (Deuteronomy 28:27, 60). Amos 4:10 has God say, "I sent a plague among you, the kind Egypt had."
sections.refs: Psalm 78:43–51; Psalm 105:26–36; 1 Samuel 4:8; 1 Samuel 6:6; Deuteronomy 28:27; Deuteronomy 28:60; Amos 4:10

sections.b: Revelation reuses the Egyptian plagues for the judgment of the whole world. The trumpets bring hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness and locusts (Revelation 8–9), and the bowls bring sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, darkness, evil spirits that look like frogs, and giant hail (Revelation 16). The victors by the sea of glass sing the song of Moses (Revelation 15:2–4). Wisdom of Solomon 11–19 retells the plagues as a long meditation on how God punishes by the very things through which people sin.
sections.refs: Revelation 8:7–12; Revelation 9:1–11; Revelation 15:2–4; Revelation 16:2–21; Wisdom of Solomon 11:5–16
